final_answer: CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing begins with a guide RNA (gRNA) designed to match a specific DNA sequence. The gRNA binds to the Cas9 enzyme, forming a complex that locates the target DNA site. The Cas9 enzyme then recognizes a short DNA sequence adjacent to the target called the PAM (protospacer adjacent motif), allowing it to bind to the DNA. Once bound, Cas9 makes a double-strand break (DSB) at the target site. The cell repairs this break through two primary mechanisms: non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), which often introduces small insertions or deletions (indels), or homology-directed repair (HDR), which can precisely repair or replace DNA sequences using a provided template. This process enables targeted gene editing. Safe.
